entries.20a3ef98ffd2d22afb6223bd7dd410e84fdce101: <div sID="gen8044" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="2Chr.6" sID="2Chr.6"/> <div eID="gen8044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8045" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8046" type="x-p"/> The glory of the Lord, in the vehicle of a thick cloud, having filled the house which Solomon built, by which God manifested his presence there, he immediately improves the opportunity, and addresses God, as a God now, in a peculiar manner, nigh at hand. I. He makes a solemn declaration of his intention in building this house, to the satisfaction of the people and the honour of God, both of whom he blessed, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.1-2Chr.6.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. He makes a solemn prayer to God that he would please graciously to accept and answer all the prayers that should be made in, or towards, that house, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.12-2Chr.6.42">ver. 12-42</reference>. This whole chapter we had before, with very little variation (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.12-1Kgs.8.53">1 Kings viii. 12-53</reference>), to which it may not be amiss here to look back.
entries.19a36865bc071068d5415cf5bfe1c97ef47819d5: <div eID="gen8046" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8045" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Solomon's Prayer to God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1004.)</title> <div sID="gen8047" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then said Solomon, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath said that he would dwell in the thick darkness. <hi type="super">2</hi> But I have built a house of habitation for thee, and a place for thy dwelling for ever. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the king turned his face, and blessed the whole congregation of Israel: and all the congregation of Israel stood. <hi type="super">4</hi> And he said, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, who hath with his hands fulfilled <hi type="italic">that</hi> which he spake with his mouth to my father David, saying, <hi type="super">5</hi> Since the day that I brought forth my people out of the land of Egypt I chose no city among all the tribes of Israel to build a house in, that my name might be there; neither chose I any man to be a ruler over my people Israel: <hi type="super">6</hi> But I have chosen Jerusalem, that my name might be there; and have chosen David to be over my people Israel. <hi type="super">7</hi> Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel. <hi type="super">8</hi> But the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said to David my father, Forasmuch as it was in thine heart to build a house for my name, thou didst well in that it was in thine heart: <hi type="super">9</hi> Notwithstanding thou shalt not build the house; but thy son which shall come forth out of thy loins, he shall build the house for my name. <hi type="super">10</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> therefore hath performed his word that he hath spoken: for I am risen up in the room of David my father, and am set on the throne of Israel, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> promised, and have built the house for the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel. <hi type="super">11</hi> And in it have I put the ark, wherein <hi type="italic">is</hi> the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that he made with the children of Israel. <div eID="gen8047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8048" type="x-p"/> It is of great consequence, in all our religious actions, that we design well, and that our eye be single. If Solomon had built this temple in the pride of his heart, as Ahasuerus made his feast, only to <hi type="italic">show the riches of his kingdom and the honour of his majesty,</hi> it would not have turned at all to his account. But here he declares upon what inducements he undertook it, and they are such as not only justify, but magnify, the undertaking. 1. He did it for the glory and honour of God; this was his highest and ultimate end in it. It was <hi type="italic">for the name of the Lord God of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.10">v. 10</reference>), to be <hi type="italic">a house of habitation for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.2">v. 2</reference>. He has indeed, as to us, <hi type="italic">made darkness his pavilion</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.1">v. 1</reference>), but let this house be the residence of that darkness; for it is in the upper world that he dwells in light, such as no eye can approach. 2. He did it in compliance with the choice God had been pleased to make of Jerusalem, to be the city in which he would record his name (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have chosen Jerusalem.</hi> A great many stately buildings there were in Jerusalem for the king, his princes, and the royal family. If God chooses that place, it is fit that there be a building for him which may excel all the rest. If men were thus honoured there, let God be thus honoured. 3. He did it in pursuance of his father's good intentions, which he never had an opportunity to put into execution: "<hi type="italic">It was in the heart of David my father to build a house for God;</hi>" the project was his, be it known, to his honour (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.7">v. 7</reference>), and God approved of it, though he permitted him not to put it in execution (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou didst well that it was in thy heart.</hi> Temple-work is often thus done; one sows and another reaps (<reference osisRef="John.4.37-John.4.38">John iv. 37, 38</reference>), one age begins that which the next brings to perfection. And let not the wisest of men think it any disparagement to them to pursue the good designs which those that went before them have laid, and to build upon their foundation. Every good piece is not an original. 4. He did it in performance of the word which God had spoken. God had said, <hi type="italic">Thy son shall build the house for my name;</hi> and now he had done it, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.9-2Chr.6.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. The service was appointed him, and the honour of it designed him, by the divine promise; so that he did not do it of his own head, but was called of God to do it. It is fit that he who appoints the work should have the appointing of the workmen; and those may go on in their work with great satisfaction who see their call to it clear.
entries.e45a21cd30311c5699169a70b4cca362b5146c6a: <div eID="gen8048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8049" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And he stood before the altar of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the presence of all the congregation of Israel, and spread forth his hands: <hi type="super">13</hi> For Solomon had made a brasen scaffold, of five cubits long, and five cubits broad, and three cubits high, and had set it in the midst of the court: and upon it he stood, and kneeled down upon his knees before all the congregation of Israel, and spread forth his hands toward heaven, <hi type="super">14</hi> And said, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of Israel, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no God like thee in the heaven, nor in the earth; which keepest covenant, and <hi type="italic">showest</hi> mercy unto thy servants, that walk before thee with all their hearts: <hi type="super">15</hi> Thou which hast kept with thy servant David my father that which thou hast promised him; and spakest with thy mouth, and hast fulfilled <hi type="italic">it</hi> with thine hand, as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> this day. <hi type="super">16</hi> Now therefore, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of Israel, keep with thy servant David my father that which thou hast promised him, saying, There shall not fail thee a man in my sight to sit upon the throne of Israel; yet so that thy children take heed to their way to walk in my law, as thou hast walked before me. <hi type="super">17</hi> Now then, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of Israel, let thy word be verified, which thou hast spoken unto thy servant David. <hi type="super">18</hi> But will God in very deed dwell with men on the earth? behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house which I have built! <hi type="super">19</hi> Have respect therefore to the prayer of thy servant, and to his supplication, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> my God, to hearken unto the cry and the prayer which thy servant prayeth before thee: <hi type="super">20</hi> That thine eyes may be open upon this house day and night, upon the place whereof thou hast said that thou wouldest put thy name there; to hearken unto the prayer which thy servant prayeth toward this place. <hi type="super">21</hi> Hearken therefore unto the supplications of thy servant, and of thy people Israel, which they shall make toward this place: hear thou from thy dwelling place, <hi type="italic">even</hi> from heaven; and when thou hearest, forgive. <hi type="super">22</hi> If a man sin against his neighbour, and an oath be laid upon him to make him swear, and the oath come before thine altar in this house; <hi type="super">23</hi> Then hear thou from heaven, and do, and judge thy servants, by requiting the wicked, by recompensing his way upon his own head; and by justifying the righteous, by giving him according to his righteousness. <hi type="super">24</hi> And if thy people Israel be put to the worse before the enemy, because they have sinned against thee; and shall return and confess thy name, and pray and make supplication before thee in this house; <hi type="super">25</hi> Then hear thou from the heavens, and forgive the sin of thy people Israel, and bring them again unto the land which thou gavest to them and to their fathers. <hi type="super">26</hi> When the heaven is shut up, and there is no rain, because they have sinned against thee; <hi type="italic">yet</hi> if they pray toward this place, and confess thy name, and turn from their sin, when thou dost afflict them; <hi type="super">27</hi> Then hear thou from heaven, and forgive the sin of thy servants, and of thy people Israel, when thou hast taught them the good way, wherein they should walk; and send rain upon thy land, which thou hast given unto thy people for an inheritance. <hi type="super">28</hi> If there be dearth in the land, if there be pestilence, if there be blasting, or mildew, locusts, or caterpillars; if their enemies besiege them in the cities of their land; whatsoever sore or whatsoever sickness <hi type="italic">there be:</hi> <hi type="super">29</hi> <hi type="italic">Then</hi> what prayer <hi type="italic">or</hi> what supplication soever shall be made of any man, or of all thy people Israel, when every one shall know his own sore and his own grief, and shall spread forth his hands in this house: <hi type="super">30</hi> Then hear thou from heaven thy dwelling place, and forgive, and render unto every man according unto all his ways, whose heart thou knowest; (for thou only knowest the hearts of the children of men:) <hi type="super">31</hi> That they may fear thee, to walk in thy ways, so long as they live in the land which thou gavest unto our fathers. <hi type="super">32</hi> Moreover concerning the stranger, which is not of thy people Israel, but is come from a far country for thy great name's sake, and thy mighty hand, and thy stretched out arm; if they come and pray in this house; <hi type="super">33</hi> Then hear thou from the heavens, <hi type="italic">even</hi> from thy dwelling place, and do according to all that the stranger calleth to thee for; that all people of the earth may know thy name, and fear thee, as <hi type="italic">doth</hi> thy people Israel, and may know that this house which I have built is called by thy name. <hi type="super">34</hi> If thy people go out to war against their enemies by the way that thou shalt send them, and they pray unto thee toward this city which thou hast chosen, and the house which I have built for thy name; <hi type="super">35</hi> Then hear thou from the heavens their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause. <hi type="super">36</hi> If they sin against thee, (for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no man which sinneth not,) and thou be angry with them, and deliver them over before <hi type="italic">their</hi> enemies, and they carry them away captives unto a land far off or near; <hi type="super">37</hi> Yet <hi type="italic">if</hi> they bethink themselves in the land whither they are carried captive, and turn and pray unto thee in the land of their captivity, saying, We have sinned, we have done amiss, and have dealt wickedly; <hi type="super">38</hi> If they return to thee with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their captivity, whither they have carried them captives, and pray toward their land, which thou gavest unto their fathers, and <hi type="italic">toward</hi> the city which thou hast chosen, and toward the house which I have built for thy name: <hi type="super">39</hi> Then hear thou from the heavens, <hi type="italic">even</hi> from thy dwelling place, their prayer and their supplications, and maintain their cause, and forgive thy people which have sinned against thee. <hi type="super">40</hi> Now, my God, let, I beseech thee, thine eyes be open, and <hi type="italic">let</hi> thine ears <hi type="italic">be</hi> attent unto the prayer <hi type="italic">that is made</hi> in this place. <hi type="super">41</hi> Now therefore arise, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God, into thy resting place, thou, and the ark of thy strength: let thy priests, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God, be clothed with salvation, and let thy saints rejoice in goodness. <hi type="super">42</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God, turn not away the face of thine anointed: remember the mercies of David thy servant. <div eID="gen8049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8050" type="x-p"/> Solomon had, in the foregoing verses, signed and sealed, as it were, the deed of dedication, by which the temple was appropriated to the honour and service of God. Now here he prays the consecration-prayer, by which it was made a figure of Christ, the great Mediator, through whom we are to offer all our prayers, and to expect all God's favours, and to whom we are to have an eye in every thing where we have to do with God. We have opened the particulars of this prayer (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.12-1Kgs.8.53">1 Kings viii.</reference>) and therefore shall now only glean up some few passages in it which may be the proper subjects of our meditation. <div eID="gen8050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8051" type="x-p"/> I. Here are some doctrinal truths occasionally laid down. As, 1. That the God of Israel is a being of incomparable perfection. We cannot describe him; but this we know, there is <hi type="italic">none like him in heaven or in earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.14">v. 14</reference>. All the creatures have their fellow-creatures, but the Creator has not his peer. He is infinitely above all, and <hi type="italic">over all, God blessed for ever.</hi> 2. That he is, and will be, true to every word that he has spoken; and all that serve him in sincerity shall certainly find him both faithful and kind. Those that set God always before them, and <hi type="italic">walk before him with all their hearts,</hi> shall find him as good as his word and better; he will both keep covenant with them and show mercy to them, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.14">v. 14</reference>. 3. That he is a being infinite and immense, whom the heaven, and heaven of heavens, cannot contain, and to whose felicity nothing is added by the utmost we can do in his service, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.18">v. 18</reference>. He is infinitely beyond the bounds of the creation and infinitely above the praises of all intelligent creatures. 4. That he, and <hi type="italic">he only, knows the hearts of the children of men,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.30">v. 30</reference>. All men's thoughts, aims, and affections, are naked and open before him; and, however the imaginations and intents of our hearts may be concealed from men, angels, and devils, they cannot be hidden from God, who knows not only what is in the heart, but the heart itself and all the beatings of it. 5. That there is no such thing as a sinless perfection to be found in this life (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is no man who sinneth not;</hi> nay, who <hi type="italic">doeth good and sinneth not;</hi> so he writes, agreeable to what he here says, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.20">Eccl. vii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen8051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8052" type="x-p"/> II. Here are some suppositions or cases put which are to be taken notice of. 1. He supposed that if doubts and controversies arose between man and man both sides would agree to appeal to God, and lay an oath upon the person whose testimony must decide the matter, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.22">v. 22</reference>. The religious reverence of an oath, as it was ancient, so, it may be presumed, it will continue as long as there are any remains of conscience and right reason among men. 2. He supposed that, though Israel enjoyed a profound peace and tranquillity, yet troublesome times would come. He did not think the mountain of their prosperity stood so strong but that it might be moved; nay, he expected sin would move it. 3. He supposed that those who had not called upon God at other times, yet, in their affliction, would seek him early and earnestly. "When they are in distress they will confess their sins, and confess thy name, and make supplication to thee." Trouble will drive those to God who have said to him, Depart, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.24">v. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.26">26</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.28">28</reference>. 4. He supposed that strangers would come from afar to worship the God of Israel and to pay homage to him; and this also might reasonably be expected, considering what worthless things the gods of the nations were, and what proofs the God of Israel had given of his being Lord of the whole earth. <div eID="gen8052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8053" type="x-p"/> III. Here are petitions very pertinent. 1. That God would own this house, and have an eye to it, as the place of which he had said that he would put his name there, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.20">v. 20</reference>. He could not, in faith, have asked God to show such peculiar favour to this house above any other if he himself had not said that it should be his rest for ever. The prayer that will speed must be warranted by the word. We may with humble confidence pray to God to be well pleased with us in Jesus Christ, because he had declared himself well pleased in him—<hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son;</hi> but he says not now of any house, "This is my beloved place." 2. That God would hear and accept the prayers which should be made in or towards that place, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.21">v. 21</reference>. He asked not that God should help them whether they prayed for themselves or no, but that God would help them in answer to their prayers. Even Christ's intercessions do not supersede but encourage our supplications. He prayed that God would hear from his dwelling-place, even from heaven. Heaven in his dwelling-place still, not this temple; and thence help must come. <hi type="italic">When thou hearest forgive.</hi> Note, The forgiveness of our sins is that which makes way for all the other answers to our prayers, <hi type="italic">Removendo prohibens—The evil which it drives away it keeps away.</hi> 3. That God would give judgment according to equity upon all the appeals that should be made to him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.23">v. 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.30">30</reference>. This we may, in faith, pray for, for we are sure it shall be done. God sitteth on the throne judging right. 4. That God would return in mercy to his people when they repented, and reformed, and sought unto him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.25">v. 25</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.27">27</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.38">38,</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.39">39</reference>. This we also may, in faith, pray for, building upon the repeated declarations God has made of his readiness to accepts penitents. 5. That God would bid the strangers welcome to this house, and answer their prayers (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.33">v. 33</reference>); for, if there be in duty, why should there not be in privilege one law for the stranger and for one born in the land? <reference osisRef="Lev.24.22">Lev. xxiv. 22</reference>. 6. That God would, upon all occasions, own and plead the cause of his people Israel, against all the opposers of it (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">Maintain their cause;</hi> and again, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.39">v. 39</reference>. If they be the Israel of God, their cause is the cause of God, and he would espouse it. 7. He concludes this prayer with some expressions which he had learned of his good father, and borrowed from one of his psalms. We had then not in the Kings, but here we have them, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.41-2Chr.6.42">v. 41, 42</reference>. The whole word of God is of use to direct us in prayer; and how can we express ourselves in better language to God than that of his own Spirit? But these words were of use, in a special manner, to direct Solomon, because they had reference to this very work that he was now doing. We have them, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.8-Ps.132.10">Ps. cxxxii. 8-10</reference>. He prayed (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.41">v. 41</reference>), (1.) That God would take possession of the temple, and keep possession, that he would make it his resting-place: <hi type="italic">Thou and the ark;</hi> what will the ark do without the God of the ark-ordinances without the God of the ordinances? (2.) That he would make the ministers of the temple public blessings: <hi type="italic">Clothe them with salvation,</hi> that is, not only save them, but make them instrumental to save others, by offering the sacrifices of righteousness. (3.) That the service of the temple might turn abundantly to the joy and satisfaction of all the Lord's people: <hi type="italic">Let thy saints rejoice in goodness,</hi> that is, in the <hi type="italic">goodness of thy house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.65.4">Ps. lxv. 4</reference>. "Let all that come hither to worship, like the eunuch, go away rejoicing." He pleads two things, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.42">v. 42</reference>. [1.] His own relation to God: "<hi type="italic">Turn not away the face of thy anointed.</hi> Lord, thou hast appointed me to be king, and wilt not thou own me?" [2.] God's covenant with his father: <hi type="italic">Remember thy mercies of David thy servant</hi>—the <hi type="italic">piety</hi> of David towards God (so some understand it and so the word sometimes signifies), his pious care of the ark, and concern for it (see <reference osisRef="Ps.132.1-Ps.132.2">Ps. cxxxii. 1, 2</reference>, &c.), or the <hi type="italic">promises</hi> of God to David, which were mercies to him, his great support and comforts in all his troubles. We may plead, as Solomon does here, with an eye to Christ:—"We deserve that God should turn away our face, that he should reject us and our prayers; but we come in the name of the Lord Jesus, <hi type="italic">thy anointed, thy Messiah</hi> (so the word is), <hi type="italic">thy Christ,</hi> so the LXX. Him thou hearest always, and wilt never <hi type="italic">turn away his face.</hi> We have no righteousness of our own to plead, but, Lord, <hi type="italic">remember the mercies of David thy servant.</hi>" Christ is God's servant (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>), and is called <hi type="italic">David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Hos. iii. 5</reference>. "Lord, remember his mercies, and accept us on the account of them. Remember his tender concern for his Father's honour and man's salvation, and what he did and suffered from that principle. Remember the promises of the everlasting covenant, which free grace has made to us in Christ, and which are called <hi type="italic">the sure mercies of David,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa. lv. 3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Acts.13.34">Acts xiii. 34</reference>. This must be all our desire and all our hope, all our prayer and all our plea; for it is all our salvation.  <chapter eID="2Chr.6"/> <div eID="gen8053" type="x-p"/>

entries.292532b28c30206804f7ee5e85db45f7cb7f51ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3950"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <div sID="gen5695" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.1-2Chr.6.41">2Ch 6:1-41</reference>. Solomon Blesses the People and Praises God.<div eID="gen5695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5696" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3950"/><hi type="bold">1. The Lord hath said that he would dwell in the thick darkness--</hi>This introduction to Solomon's address was evidently suggested by the remarkable incident recorded at the close of the last chapter: the phenomenon of a densely opaque and uniformly shaped cloud, descending in a slow and majestic manner and filling the whole area of the temple. He regarded it himself, and directed the people also to regard it, as an undoubted sign and welcome pledge of the divine presence and acceptance of the building reared to His honor and worship. He referred not to any particular declaration of God, but to the cloud having been all along in the national history of Israel the recognized symbol of the divine presence (<reference osisRef="Exod.16.10">Ex 16:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.24.16">24:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.40.34">40:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.9.15">Nu 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.10">1Ki 8:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.11">11</reference>). <div eID="gen5696" type="x-p"/>
entries.08dd39409da1d247dc41a60b70129ae50b1ffc0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3951"/><div sID="gen5697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3951"/><hi type="bold">13. Solomon had made a brazen scaffold--</hi>a sort of platform. But the Hebrew term rendered "scaffold," being the same as that used to designate the basin, suggests the idea that this throne might bear some resemblance, in form or structure, to those lavers in the temple, being a sort of round and elevated pulpit, placed in the middle of the court, and in front of the altar of burnt offering.<div eID="gen5697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon it he stood, and kneeled down upon his knees--</hi>After ascending the brazen scaffold, he assumed those two attitudes in succession, and with different objects in view. He stood while he addressed and blessed the surrounding multitude (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.3-2Chr.6.11">2Ch 6:3-11</reference>). Afterwards he knelt down and stretched out his hands towards heaven, with his face probably turned towards the altar, while he gave utterance to the beautiful and impressive prayer which is recorded in the remainder of this chapter. It is deserving of notice that there was no seat in this pulpit--for the king either stood or knelt all the time he was in it. It is not improbable that it was surmounted by a canopy, or covered by a veil, to screen the royal speaker from the rays of the sun. <div eID="gen5698" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3b6ff8fdc8b997c31b416cde946c54e1036ebf4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3952"/><div sID="gen5699" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3952"/><hi type="bold">18-21. how much less this house which I have built! Have respect therefore to the prayer of thy servant--</hi>No person who entertains just and exalted views of the spiritual nature of the Divine Being will suppose that he can raise a temple for the habitation of Deity, as a man builds a house for himself. Nearly as improper and inadmissible is the idea that a temple can contribute to enhance the glory of God, as a monument may be raised in honor of a great man. Solomon described the true and proper use of the temple, when he entreated that the Lord would "hearken unto the supplications of His servant and His people Israel, which they should make towards this place." In short, the grand purpose for which the temple was erected was precisely the same as that contemplated by churches--to afford the opportunity and means of public and social worship, according to the ritual of the Mosaic dispensation--to supplicate the divine mercy and favor--to render thanks for past instances of goodness, and offer petitions for future blessings (see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.22">1Ki 8:22</reference>). This religious design of the temple--the ONE temple in the world--is in fact its standpoint of absorbing interest. <div eID="gen5699" type="x-p"/>
entries.f624324518bdfcd3fdcd5540ec186d011e922027: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3953"/><div sID="gen5700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3953"/><hi type="bold">22. If a man sin against his neighbour, and an oath be laid upon him to make him swear, and the oath come before thine altar in this house, &c.--</hi>In cases where the testimony of witnesses could not be obtained and there was no way of settling a difference or dispute between two people but by accepting the oath of the accused, the practice had gradually crept in and had acquired the force of consuetudinary law, for the party to be brought before the altar, where his oath was taken with all due solemnity, together with the imprecation of a curse to fall upon himself if his disavowal should be found untrue. There is an allusion to such a practice in this passage. <div eID="gen5700" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9551125c3bd85e658cdc711fe0fe018783fe566: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3954"/><div sID="gen5701" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3954"/><hi type="bold">38. If they return to thee ... in the land of their captivity ... and pray toward their land, which thou gavest unto their fathers--</hi>These words gave rise to the favorite usage of the ancient as well as modern Jews, of turning in prayer toward Jerusalem, in whatever quarter of the world they might be, and of directing their faces toward the temple when in Jerusalem itself or in any part of the holy land (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.44">1Ki 8:44</reference>). <div eID="gen5701" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e8e2ec99b4fa474e9d1a7800d6273b234127da2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3955"/><div sID="gen5702" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3955"/><hi type="bold">41. arise, O Lord God into thy resting-place--</hi>These words are not found in the record of this prayer in the First Book of Kings; but they occur in <reference osisRef="Ps.132.8">Psa 132:8</reference>, which is generally believed to have been composed by David, or rather by Solomon, in reference to this occasion. "Arise" is a very suitable expression to be used when the ark was to be removed from the tabernacle in Zion to the temple on Mount Moriah.<div eID="gen5702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into thy resting-place--</hi>the temple so called (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.1">Is 66:1</reference>), because it was a fixed and permanent mansion (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.14">Psa 132:14</reference>).<div eID="gen5703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the ark of thy strength--</hi>the abode by which Thy glorious presence is symbolized, and whence Thou dost issue Thine authoritative oracles, and manifest Thy power on behalf of Thy people when they desire and need it. It might well be designated the ark of God's strength, because it was through means of it the mighty miracles were wrought and the brilliant victories were won, that distinguish the early annals of the Hebrew nation. The sight of it inspired the greatest animation in the breasts of His people, while it diffused terror and dismay through the ranks of their enemies (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.78.61">Psa 78:61</reference>).<div eID="gen5704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let thy priests ... be clothed with salvation--</hi>or with righteousness (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.9">Psa 132:9</reference>), that is, be equipped not only with the pure white linen garments Thou hast appointed for their robe of office, but also adorned with the moral beauties of true holiness, that their person and services may be accepted, both for themselves and all the people. Thus they would be "clothed with salvation," for that is the effect and consequence of a sanctified character. <div eID="gen5705" type="x-p"/>
entries.cdb76669ad04273f50266b11bd5988358aef5085: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3956"/><div sID="gen5706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3956"/><hi type="bold">42. turn not away the face of thine anointed--</hi>that is, of me, who by Thy promise and appointment have been installed as king and ruler of Israel. The words are equivalent in meaning to this: Do not reject my present petitions; do not send me from Thy throne of grace dejected in countenance and disappointed in heart.<div eID="gen5706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5707" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remember the mercies of David thy servant--</hi>that is, the mercies promised to David, and in consideration of that promise, hear and answer my prayer (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.132.10">Psa 132:10</reference>). <chapter eID="2Chr.6"/>

entries.bae8046f1d76befa8fbc2bccc140d9e0133fcd05: <div eID="gen14025" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14026" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14027" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14027" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14026" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14028" type="x-p"/> Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple, vv. 1-42. <div eID="gen14028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14029" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen14029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14030" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath said that he would dwell - Solomon, seeing the cloud descend and fill the house, immediately took for granted that the Lord had accepted the place, and was now present. What occurred now was precisely the same with what took place when Moses reared the tabernacle in the wilderness; see <reference osisRef="Exo.40.34">Exo 40:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.40.35">Exo 40:35</reference> : A cloud covered the tent - and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter into the tent - because the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle. <div eID="gen14030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14031" type="x-p"/> The Chaldee paraphrases thus: "Then said Solomon, It has pleased God to place his majesty in the city of Jerusalem, in the house of the sanctuary which I have built to the name of his Word, and he hath placed a dark cloud before him.
entries.904a627f17edfc43bfc362cd5a5b3367fd681ffa: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen14031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14032" type="x-p"/> For the name of the Lord - "For the name of the Word of the Lord God of Israel." - Targum.
entries.b8aff6479f6dbb035176b21fa24724a480173611: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen14032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14033" type="x-p"/> That walk before thee with all their hearts - "With all the will of their souls and with all the affection of their hearts." - Targum.
entries.f1217aabd411e84b3c7e05df9da1a65309f716cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen14033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14034" type="x-p"/> But will God in very deed dwell with men - "But who could have imagined, who could have thought it credible, that God should place his majesty among men dwelling upon earth? Behold, the highest heavens, the middle heavens, and the lowest heavens, cannot bear the glory of thy majesty, (for thou art the God who sustainest all the heavens, and the earth, and the deep, and all that is in them), nor can this house which I have built contain Thee." - Targum.
entries.1827c7516e4e244645ac5113241f111943ffdaac: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen14034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14035" type="x-p"/> If a man sin against his neighbor - For the Seven cases put here by Solomon in his prayer, see the notes on 1 Kings 8:31-46 (note).
entries.659ecae9a978ccad21be130f6024f8fa95dec48f: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen14035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14036" type="x-p"/> For there is no man which sinneth not - See this case largely considered in the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.46">1Kgs 8:46</reference> (note).
entries.ca4ab231ed8c60c7e2e8865e90b4f9e4201f372c: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen14036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14037" type="x-p"/> If they bethink themselves - "If thy fear should return into their hearts." - Targum. <div eID="gen14037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14038" type="x-p"/> The whole of this prayer is amply considered in the parallel place, 1 Kings 8:22-53 (note), where see the notes.

entries.37a260ff1789606ed59d086bb88b630019a17709: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen14039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14040" type="x-p"/> Turn not away the face of thine anointed - "At least do me good; and if not for my sake, do it for thy own sake." - Jarchi. <div eID="gen14040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14041" type="x-p"/> These two last verses are not in the parallel place in 1 Kings 8:22-53. entries.ac4d522544783eb761c0a5d3584a38c3163492fc: <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.1-2Chr.6.11">2Ch 6:1-11</reference> <div eID="gen5951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5952" type="x-p"/> The words with which Solomon celebrates this wondrous evidence of the divine favour, entirely coincide with the narrative in 1Ki 8:12-21, except that in 2Ch 6:5. the actual words of Solomon’s speech are more completely given than in 1Ki 8:16, where the words, “and I have not chosen a man to be prince over my people Israel, and I have chosen Jerusalem that my name might be there,” are omitted. For the commentary on this address, see on 1Ki 8:12-21.
entries.cd24036ef40a627c1d2a365e6afa098f2e68368f: <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.12-2Chr.6.42">2Ch 6:12-42</reference> <hi type="italic">Solomon’s dedicatory prayer</hi> likewise corresponds exactly with the account of it given in 1 Kings 8:22-53 till near the end (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.40-2Chr.6.42">2Ch 6:40-42</reference>), where it takes quite a different turn. Besides this, in the introduction (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.13">2Ch 6:13</reference>) Solomon’s position during the prayer is more accurately described, it being there stated that Solomon had caused a high stage (כּיּור, a basin-like elevation) to be erected, which he ascended, and kneeling, spoke the prayer which follows. This fact is not stated in 1Ki 8:22, and Then. and Berth. conjecture that it has been dropped out of our text only by mistake. Perhaps so, but it may have been passed over by the author of the books of Kings as a point of subordinate importance. On the contents of the prayer, which begins with the joyful confession that the Lord had fulfilled His promise to David in reference to the building of the temple, and proceeds with a request for a further bestowment of the blessing promised to His people, and a supplication that all prayers made to the Lord in the temple may be heard, see the Com. on 1Ki 8:22. The conclusion of the prayer in the Chronicle is different from that in 1 Kings 8. There the last supplication, that the prayers might be heard, is followed by the thought: for they (the Israelites) are Thy people and inheritance; and in the further amplification of this thought the prayer returns to the idea with which it commenced. In the narrative of the Chronicle, on the other hand, the supplications conclude with the general thought (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.40">2Ch 6:40</reference>): “Now, my God, let, I beseech Thee, Thine eyes be open, and Thine ears attend unto the prayer of this place” (i.e., unto the prayer spoken in this place). There follows, then, the conclusion of the whole prayer - a summons to the Lord (2Ch 6:41.): “And now, Lord God, arise into Thy rest, Thou and the ark of Thy strength; let Thy priests, Lord God, clothe themselves in salvation, and Thy saints rejoice in good! Lord God, turn not away the face of Thine anointed: remember the pious deeds of Thy servant David.” הסדים as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.32">2Ch 32:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.26">2Ch 35:26</reference>, and Neh 13:14. On this Thenius remarks, to 1Ki 8:53 : “This conclusion is probably authentic, for there is in the text of the prayer, 1 Kings 8, no special expression of dedication, and this the summons to enter into possession of the temple very fittingly supplies. The whole contents of the conclusion are in perfect correspondence with the situation, and, as to form, nothing better could be desired. It can scarcely be thought an arbitrary addition made by the chronicler for no other reason than that the summons spoken of, if taken literally, is irreconcilable with the entrance of the cloud into the temple, of which he has already given us an account.” Berth. indeed thinks that it does not thence follow that our conclusion is authentic, and considers it more probable that it was introduced because it appeared more suitable, in place of the somewhat obscure words in 1Ki 8:51-53, though not by the author of the Chronicle, and scarcely at an earlier time. The decision on this question can only be arrived at in connection with the question as to the origin of the statements peculiar to the Chronicle contained in <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.1">2Ch 7:1</reference>-3. <div eID="gen5952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5953" type="x-p"/> If we consider, in the first place, our verses in themselves, they contain no thought which Solomon might not have spoken, and consequently nothing which would tend to show that they are not authentic. It is true that the phrase קשּׁבות אזניך occurs only here and in <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.15">2Ch 7:15</reference>, and again in <reference osisRef="Ps.130.2">Psa 130:2</reference>, and the noun נוּח instead of מנוּחה is found only in <reference osisRef="Esth.9.16-Esth.9.18">Est 9:16-18</reference> in the form נוח; but even if these two expressions be peculiar to the later time, no further conclusion can be drawn from that, than that the author of the Chronicle has here, as often elsewhere, given the thoughts of his authority in the language of his own time. Nor is the relation in which <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.41">2Ch 6:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.42">2Ch 6:42</reference> stand to <reference osisRef="Ps.132.8-Ps.132.10">Psa 132:8-10</reference> a valid proof of the later composition of the conclusion of our prayer. For (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) it is still a question whether our verses have been borrowed from Ps 132, or the verses of the psalm from our passage; and (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) the period when <reference osisRef="Ps.138.1-Ps.138.8">Psa 138:1-8</reference> was written is so doubtful, that some regard it as a Solomonic psalm, while others place it in the post-exilic period. Neither the one nor the other of these questions can be determined on convincing grounds. The appeal to the fact that the chronicler has compounded the hymn in 1 Chron 15 also out of post-exilic psalms proves nothing, for even in that case it is at least doubtful if that be a correct account of the matter. But the further assertion, that the conclusion (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.42">2Ch 6:42</reference>) resembles <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa 55:3</reference>, and that recollections of this passage may have had some effect also on the conclusion (<reference osisRef="2Chr.6.41">2Ch 6:41</reference>), is undoubtedly erroneous, for דויד חסדי in <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.42">2Ch 6:42</reference> has quite a different meaning from that which it has in Isa 55:3. There דּוד חסדי are the favours granted to David by the Lord; in <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.42">2Ch 6:42</reference>, on the contrary, they are the pious deeds of David, - all that he had done for the raising and advancement of the public worship (see above). The phrase וגו קוּמה, “Arise, O Lord God, into Thy rest,” is modelled on the formula which was spoken when the ark was lifted and when it was set down on the journey through the wilderness, which explains both קוּמה and the use of לנוּחך, which is formed after בּנוּחה, Num 10:36. The call to arise into rest is not inconsistent with the fact that the ark had already been brought into the most holy place, for קוּמה has merely the general signification, “to set oneself to anything.” The idea is, that God would now take the rest to which the throne of His glory had attained, show Himself to His people from this His throne to be the God of salvation, endue His priests, the guardians of His sanctuary, with salvation, and cause the pious to rejoice in His goodness. בטּוב ישׂמחוּ is generalized in <reference osisRef="Ps.132.9">Psa 132:9</reference> into ירנּנוּ. פּני פ השׁב, to turn away the face of any one, i.e., to deny the request, cf. 1Ki 2:16.<hi type="italic">The divine confirmation of the dedication of the temple</hi>. - <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.1">2Ch 7:1</reference>-10. The consecration of the sacrificial service by fire from heaven (<reference osisRef="2Chr.7.1-2Chr.7.3">2Ch 7:1-3</reference>), and the sacrifices and festival of the people (<reference osisRef="2Chr.7.4-2Chr.7.10">2Ch 7:4-10</reference>).  <chapter eID="2Chr.6"/> <div eID="gen5953" type="x-p"/>
